# Suppavāsā Sutta (Ud 2.8 (PTS Ud 15))

**ID:** Ud 2.8 (PTS Ud 15)
**Section:** Udāna (ud)

**Title (Pali):** Suppavāsā Sutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Suppavāsā Sutta* (Ud 2.8) is the eighth discourse of the second chapter (Mucalindavagga) of the Udāna. Set at Kuṇḍiyā in the Kuṇḍadhāna Grove, the sutta relates that Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyans, had endured a pregnancy of seven years followed by seven days of acute, obstructed labor [Masefield 1997]. Despite her intense physical suffering, she maintains composure through three reflective thoughts extolling the Buddha, the Saṅgha, and Nibbāna, and dispatches her husband to convey her homage to the Blessed One [Masefield 1997]. Upon receiving the Buddha's blessing, she safely delivers her son (identified in later tradition as the future arahant Sīvali) and subsequently sponsors a seven-day meal offering for the Buddha and the monastic order [Burlingame 1921; Buswell & Lopez 2014].

Comparative analysis by modern scholars highlights the close relationship between this discourse and other early Buddhist story collections. Eugene W. Burlingame notes that while the *Udāna* account is more detailed than the *Asātarūpajātaka* (Ja 100) and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, the commentary on the Dhammapada borrows its narrative almost verbatim from the *Udāna* (Ud 15–18) [Burlingame 1921]. In both the *Udāna* and Jātaka accounts, a lay supporter of Mahāmoggallāna postpones a prearranged meal to allow the Buddha to accept Suppavāsā's invitation [Burlingame 1921]. Curated parallels for the verses or narrative include *Udānavarga* chapter 5 (*Priyavarga* / Tibetan Uv Kg 5), Chinese translations (T 210.21, T 212.6, T 213.5), and Jātaka 100. Anālayo observes that T 212 is the only Chinese *Udāna* collection preserving a prose narrative counterpart alongside the verse [Anālayo 2016]. DharmaNexus confirms extensive Pali text reuse with the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*, the Vinaya Khandhakas (Kd 1, Kd 6, Kd 15), and the Nikāyas, alongside machine alignments with the Tibetan Vinayavibhaṅga (D0003-3) and Chinese Āgamas (T 26, T 125) [DharmaNexus].
